# quality


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

Some documents in a store are noise: they match many queries and answer
none. A scraped cookie banner, a navigation menu or a licence footer
shows up in search results because its words are common, and it pushes
real answers down the list. This module gives every document a noise
score so you can find such documents and decide whether to remove them.

The score needs no labelled examples, no extra model and no second pass
over the source files. It is computed from the chunk vectors and texts
the store already holds. A cookie banner gives itself away in several
ways at once: near-identical copies of it appear on many pages, its
vector sits away from most of the corpus, and its words are ones that
occur everywhere.

The default weights were measured in vishalakshi (`evals/noise.py` and
`evals/RESULTS.md` in that repository) on three test corpora with
boilerplate documents planted in them. The weighted score separated
boilerplate from real documents with a mean AUC of 0.988 (0.967 to
1.000). AUC is the chance that a randomly chosen noise document scores
above a randomly chosen real one, so 0.5 is a coin toss and 1.0 is
perfect.

The functions read a tree store, the kind
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) and
`add_doc` build, because they need each chunk’s
[`doc_id`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/tree.html#doc_id) and
the `docs` table for titles. A plain `get_store` table has neither.

## The vectors, as one array

`chunk_matrix` reads every chunk that has an embedding and returns its
id, its document id, its text and its vector, with the vectors stacked
into one float32 array and scaled to unit length. With unit vectors, a
dot product is the cosine similarity. Pass `limit` to work on a random
sample of chunks in a large store, and `dtype` if the store holds
vectors in a width other than float16.

``` python
def chunk_matrix(

    limit:int=None, # sample this many chunks instead of using all of them
    seed:int=0, # random seed for the sample
    dtype:type=float16, # the width the store holds
)->tuple:
```

*Return `(ids, doc_ids, texts, V)` for every chunk with an embedding,
with `V` the unit-length vectors as one float32 array.*

## Nearest neighbours, centroids and word rarity

These helpers compute the quantities the features are built from.
[`_knn`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/quality.html#_knn)
finds each chunk’s nearest other chunks: exactly, by matrix product, up
to 30,000 chunks, and through a temporary HNSW index above that, unless
usearch’s HNSW index failed its probe.
[`_centroids`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/quality.html#_centroids)
finds topic centres with k-means.
[`chunk_idf`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/quality.html#chunk_idf)
splits text into words with `TOKEN_RE` and scores how rare each word is
across chunks: inverse document frequency (IDF) is high for a word few
chunks use and near zero for a word in nearly every chunk.
[`_entropy`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/quality.html#_entropy)
measures how evenly a row of probabilities is spread, from 0 (all on one
value) to 1 (spread evenly).

## The features

[`noise_features`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/quality.html#noise_features)
computes nine numbers per document. Each is computed per chunk and
averaged over the document’s chunks, and in each a larger value means
more likely noise.

`spread_doc` and `short` are computed but weighted 0, because on their
own they scored below chance in vishalakshi’s measurements. `spread_doc`
in particular marks survey documents that cover many topics, which are
not noise.

`promiscuity` is the only feature that needs data from outside the
store: a log of which queries retrieved which documents, passed as
`seen`, a dict from doc id to the set of queries. Without it the feature
is 0 for every document and the other eight decide the score.

[`noise_scores`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/quality.html#noise_scores)
turns the features into one score per document and returns every
document, most likely noise first, with its title and each feature
value. Each feature is first converted to its rank among the documents
and rescaled to about -1.7 to 1.7 by
[`robust_z`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/quality.html#robust_z),
so one extreme value cannot dominate. The score is then the weighted
average using `NOISE_W`, or your own `weights`, or a fitted
[`Ranker`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/quality.html#ranker).
Ranks matter here: with plain z-scores, one outlier document on `hub`
dropped the measured AUC from 0.988 to 0.55.

### noise_features

``` python
def noise_features(
    db, # an open Database
    store:str='store', # the chunk table
    seen:dict=None, # doc_id -> the set of queries it was retrieved for, if logged
    k:int=10, # neighbours per chunk
    topics:int=64, # topic centroids for the spread features
    tau:float=0.9, # similarity floor for "this is a duplicate"
    temp:float=8.0, # softmax temperature for chunk-to-topic spread
    limit:int=None, # sample this many chunks instead of using all of them
    exact_max:int=30000, # above this many chunks, neighbours come from HNSW instead of an exact search
    seed:int=0, # random seed for sampling and k-means
    dtype:type=float16, # the width the store holds
)->fastcore.basics.AttrDict:
```

*Compute the nine noise features for every document in a tree store, as
`AttrDict(doc_ids, X, names)`.*

## The ranker

The fixed weights work without any labels. If you have marked some
documents as noise and some as keepers,
[`Ranker`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/quality.html#ranker)
learns weights from those marks instead; vishalakshi measured 0.996 AUC
that way, from six marked documents and eighteen keepers.

[`Ranker`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/quality.html#ranker)
is a pairwise learning-to-rank model. You give it rows of features, a
group for each row, and a target value. Within each group, every pair of
rows where one has the higher target becomes a training example, and the
model learns weights that score the higher row above the lower one. It
is a logistic regression on the feature differences of those pairs, with
an L2 penalty, fitted by Newton’s method (iteratively reweighted least
squares, IRLS).

For noise, put every document in one group and use 1 for noise and 0 for
keep, then pass the fitted ranker to `noise_scores(ranker=...)`.
vishalakshi also fits one on its log of search feedback, with one group
per query, to re-rank results. `weights()` shows what the model learned,
and `to_dict` and `from_dict` save and restore it as plain
JSON-compatible data.

## Tests

The tests build an
[`Index`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/api.html#index) with
five real documents and three near-copies of a cookie banner. They use
[`hash_embed`](https://Karthik777.github.io/litesearch/utils.html#hash_embed),
a hashing encoder that needs no model or network. It matches spellings
only, so it separates the banner less cleanly than a real encoder would.

``` python
from fastcore.test import test_eq, test_close
from litesearch import Index, hash_embed

class HashEmbed:
    "`hash_embed` behind an `.encode`, so these tests need no model and no network."
    def __init__(self, dims=256): self.dims = dims
    def encode(self, xs, **kw): return hash_embed(list(xs), ndim=self.dims)
```
